scores.label: fixture:cinderella
scores.notes: A faithful, beat-for-beat reproduction of the classical Perrault fairy tale. Every piece of machinery—from dramatic irony to the midnight ticking clock—is cleanly assembled and executed.

causal_pairs.why: The Prince's ball is an independent royal decree, not caused by the household remarriage or Cinderella's demotion.
The ball invitation directly causes the sisters to prepare their finery and enlist Cinderella to dress their hair.
The cruel mockery and departure of the sisters leave Cinderella alone in the emotional state that prompts her weeping.
Cinderella's solitary weeping directly summons the godmother to intervene and transform her.
The godmother's magical provision of coach, gown, and slippers enables Cinderella to arrive at the ball and stun the court.
Her successful reception at the ball flows directly into mingling with the court and her sisters before departing before midnight.
Her safe, timely return allows her to thank her godmother and request permission to attend the following night.
Cinderella's return from the ball before her sisters sets up the household interaction where they unknowingly describe her to her face.
The second ball was already arranged with the godmother in E08; the daytime conversation in E09 does not cause the ball or Cinderella's attendance.
The stroke of midnight and the sudden reversion of the magic directly force Cinderella to trek home on foot in rags.
The Prince launches the kingdom-wide search because of the lost slipper left at the palace in E10, not because Cinderella concealed the second slipper in her pocket in E11.
The systematic house-to-house search by the gentleman-in-waiting brings the trial to Cinderella's household.
The incontrovertible proof of Cinderella's identity directly causes the sisters' repentance and her marriage to the Prince.

payoffs.why: The strict midnight deadline is established as an explicit rule, tested safely on night one to establish routine, and then detonated when Cinderella loses track of time on night two.
The remaining slipper is noted in E11 purely to serve as a matching prop for the fitting in E13, performing no other narrative work in the interim.

scores.label: fixture:a-christmas-carol
scores.notes: The structure is the definitive archetype of moral reform through visionary horror and empathy. Every setup in the opening Stave finds an exact, inverted mirror in the closing resolution.

causal_pairs.why: Scrooge's obstinate greed and callous isolation in the opening scene directly precipitate Marley's ghostly intervention to warn him away from the same fate.
Marley explicitly warns Scrooge that the first spirit will appear when the bell tolls one, which directly triggers the Ghost of Christmas Past's arrival.
The Spirit physically takes Scrooge by the hand through the wall into his childhood, directly initiating the schoolroom vision.
The transition from the schoolroom to Fezziwig's party is guided by the Spirit's curated chronological tour of Scrooge's memories, not caused by the outcome of the schoolroom scene.
The shift from Fezziwig's warehouse to Belle breaking the engagement is the next stage in the Spirit's historical sequence rather than a direct result of Scrooge's reflection on Fezziwig.
Scrooge extinguishes the first Spirit in anguish and collapses back into sleep, setting up his scheduled awakening to meet the second Spirit.
The Ghost of Christmas Present leads Scrooge out into the city specifically to observe present Christmas celebrations, bringing him directly to the Cratchit home.
The Spirit transports Scrooge to bleak and remote locations to expand the vision's scope, which follows the Cratchit dinner without being triggered by it.
The movement from distant ships and lighthouses to Fred's drawing-room is another curated stop on the Spirit's itinerary.
The passage of time during the night's tour brings the Spirit to midnight and the end of its lifespan, causing it to age, reveal Ignorance and Want, and depart.
The vanishing of the second Spirit at midnight immediately summons the approaching Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come, who leads Scrooge to the Exchange.
The move from the Royal Exchange to Old Joe's shop is part of the third Spirit's episodic demonstration of the dead man's reputation.
The Spirit continues its sequential revelation by taking Scrooge from the thieves fencing the dead man's goods to the dark room where the plundered body lies.
Scrooge's inability to uncover the face and his plea to see any tenderness connected with death directly prompts the Spirit to show Caroline's household.
The Spirit transitions from the relieved debtor couple to the Cratchit family mourning Tiny Tim to present a contrasting picture of genuine grief.
Scrooge's mounting distress over these shadowy deaths impels him to demand whose fate he has been watching, prompting the Spirit to guide him to the churchyard grave.
Scrooge's complete moral capitulation and desperate vows at his own gravestone cause him to awaken transformed in his own chambers on Christmas morning.
Scrooge's ecstatic commitment to live differently immediately drives him into the street to make restitution to the charity solicitor and reconcile with Fred.
The momentum of Scrooge's Christmas Day transformation directly carries into the counting-house the next morning to permanently alter his relationship with Bob Cratchit.

payoffs.why: The callous line spoken casually in E01 as an ideological dismissal is weaponized by the Spirit in E08 against Tiny Tim, delivering a sharp moral and emotional reckoning.
The conditional warning of Tim's death in E08 is dramatically realized in E16, raising the emotional stakes of Scrooge's impending choice.
The mystery established at the outset of Stave IV sustains dramatic irony across five scenes of escalating revulsion before resolving definitively on the headstone in E17.

raw.notes: The structure is the definitive archetype of moral reform through visionary horror and empathy. Every setup in the opening Stave finds an exact, inverted mirror in the closing resolution.

Nora's claim that Derry left before 02:30 sends Maren to question Orson about when the wicket lock was secured.

Arthur calling Maren into his office to present the initialed ledger is part of his independent framing timeline, not caused by her workshop search.

Tessa convening the shift workers near Kiln 4 to discuss crew safety is scheduled by the union, not caused by Maren catching Nora falsifying logs.
Arthur exploits the crew's hostility and Maren's isolation to spring the locker search in front of the yard committee.
Maren unlocking her locker directly allows Arthur to reach in and reveal the planted scale counterweight.
The discovery of the planted murder weapon in her locker leads directly to Arthur cornering her in the manager's office to force an involuntary manslaughter confession.

scores.label: arc_structured_orchard
scores.notes: The mystery mechanics are exceptionally clean, relying on botany and contract law rather than violent contrivance. The thematic collision between legal title to timber and intellectual authorship of a cultivar provides a satisfying, costly resolution.

causal_pairs.why: Aletha's discovery of the felled orchard brings Robin out to the terrace with clearing tools to inspect the damage.
Robin's deliberate deflection toward Gervais and the boundary dispute sends an enraged Aletha directly to the weigh station to confront him.
The public argument over ownership prompts Milo to pull the historical boundary maps and reveal Gervais's pending bonus claim.
Having established Gervais's apparent financial motive, Aletha conducts an unauthorized search of his packing barn.
Gervais ejecting Aletha from the barn creates the opportunity for Beth to intercept her privately outside.

Beth's disclosure about Gervais's debt leads Aletha into broad inquiries, but Helen's testimony about pasture history occurs as general background rather than being directly triggered by Beth's words.
Believing the lantern sighting confirms Gervais's nighttime presence, Aletha returns to the cooperative office to verify his formal filings.
Examining Gervais's petition to claim the variety brings Calder into the conversation to explain the legal rules governing cultivar payouts.
Calder's rule that dead wood pays nothing creates an anomaly that drives Aletha back to the stumps to forensically examine the cuts.
The absence of blue oil on the stumps forces Aletha to confront Gervais's household regarding his exact timeline and alibi.
Refusing to accept Gervais's freight receipt alibi, Aletha doubles down and brings a formal accusation of hired sabotage to the board.
Aletha's formal accusation before the buyers compels Gervais to lay out his personal finances and confess the living tree bounty.
The collapse of Gervais's motive prompts Calder to disclose the actual punitive terms in Clause 14B.
Realizing the felling was meant to avert the Clause 14B fine, Aletha immediately checks who had read the confidential draft.
Discovering Robin signed out the contract draft leads Aletha straight to Robin's workspace in the nursery shed.
Finding the pull-saw, scions, and wax in the shed enables Aletha to directly confront Robin the moment he walks in.
Robin's confession and explanation of scion legality force Aletha to examine the cut wood and grapple with the legal dilemma.
To establish variety authorship and defeat the penalty, Aletha takes her breeding journal to Calder, which exposes Robin's crime to the cooperative.
The restitution demands by Gervais and Milo force Aletha to surrender her buyout payment to protect Robin from prosecution.

payoffs.why: This seed fact functions as immediate expository context in E01 rather than an earned dramatized setup.
Planted in the seed world, surfaced in E02, and fully deployed in E04 as the foundational justification for Aletha's defensible wrong turn.
Spotted casually in E05, the oil serves as a classic fair-play negative clue when the stump kerf test in E10 disproves Gervais's involvement.
Framed in E04 as a hostile land-grab motive, it is inverted in E13 to prove Gervais desperately needed the trees left standing.
Calder's vague corporate threat in E03 pays off in E14 when Clause 14B reveals the protective nature of the saboteur's crime.
Noted quietly as an atmospheric sensory detail at the crime scene in E02, it conclusively ties Robin's shed bench to the felling in E16.
Misattributed by Aletha in E07 to Gervais, this witness detail cleanly resolves in E17 to lock down Robin's path and timing.
A quiet seed fact that becomes the pivotal forensic pivot in E15 and E17, explaining why Robin alone acted on Clause 14B.
